subtitle: Midterm Important Subjective Questions (Solved)
topics: Mobility of DNA and Genetic Manipulation

subjective.question: Define biotechnology. Also define environmental biotechnology.
subjective.answer: Biotechnology is "the application of science and technology to living organisms, as well as parts, products and models thereof, to alter living or non-living materials for the production of knowledge, goods and services" (OECD, 2002). Environmental biotechnology is the branch of biotechnology that addresses environmental problems, such as the removal of pollution, renewable energy generation or biomass production, by exploiting biological processes.

subjective.question: What are the three key points for environmental biotechnology interventions? In what two ways can the goals of environmental biotechnology be achieved?
subjective.answer: The three key points for environmental biotechnology interventions are: (1) the manufacturing process, (2) waste management, and (3) pollution control. The goals can be achieved in two ways: (i) by enhancing or optimising conditions for existing biological systems so that their activities happen faster or more efficiently, or (ii) by resorting to some form of alteration to bring about the desired outcome.

subjective.question: Write a note on the global environmental market and its major areas.
subjective.answer: The global environmental market has shown massive growth, and it was predicted that the market would grow to 7400 billion US dollars by 2025. Driving factors include greater general awareness, widespread adoption of sustainable best practice by industry, geo-political changes and clean manufacturing applications. The major areas so far are energy production, waste management, land remediation and water treatment; water treatment alone accounts for 25% of the total global environmental market. The OECD (2001) concluded that the industrial use of biotechnology commonly leads to increasingly environmentally harmonious processes and additionally results in lowered operating and/or capital costs.

subjective.question: What conditions must be satisfied for the use of biological systems in treating a pollutant?
subjective.answer: The intended target of the bio-processing must generally be both susceptible and available to biological attack, in aqueous solution, or at least in contact with water, and within a low to medium toxicity range. For land-based applications, the soil types best suited to biotechnological interventions are sands and gravels. Nutrient availability, oxygenation and the presence of other contaminants can also play a role.

subjective.question: What are extremophiles? Why are extremozymes important?
subjective.answer: Extremophiles are microbial species that tolerate extreme conditions, such as high salinity, pressures and temperatures, e.g. the Archaea, which include extreme thermophiles, extreme halophiles, methanogens and species tolerating high levels of ionising radiation, pH or high pressures. Much of the interest centres on their enzymes, the so-called extremozymes, whose promise lies in their ability to remain functional when other enzymes cannot. Extremophiles could therefore provide a way of developing alternative routes to many conventional chemicals or materials.

subjective.question: Differentiate between thermophiles and hyperthermophiles. Give an application of thermophile enzymes.
subjective.answer: Thermophiles thrive at temperatures above 45°C, whereas hyperthermophiles thrive at still higher temperatures, around 85°C. They are found in hot springs, deep sea vents and geothermal fluids. Their enzymes are industrially important: the DNA polymerase of Thermus aquaticus (Taq polymerase) and of Pyrococcus furiosus (Pfu polymerase) are used in the polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Thermophiles are also used in clean energy applications such as bioethanol production and hydrogen production in fuel cells.

subjective.question: Write a short note on psychrophiles, halophiles, acidophiles and alkaliphiles.
subjective.answer: Psychrophiles tolerate cold environments (the average oceanic temperature is around 1-3°C and vast areas of land are permanently frozen). Halophiles survive intensely saline environments such as natural salt lakes; they keep their cytoplasm at a higher solute concentration than the surroundings by manufacturing or concentrating solutes, e.g. many accumulate KCl, so their extremozymes work only in the presence of KCl. Acidophiles thrive at low pH, typically below 5, using protective molecules in their cell walls and membranes to exclude acids; extremozymes functioning below pH 1 have been isolated. Alkaliphiles flourish at pH 9 or more, e.g. in soda lakes and heavily alkaline soils, relying on protective molecules in their surfaces or secretions.

subjective.question: What are xenobiotics? Explain gratuitous degradation and cometabolism.
subjective.answer: Xenobiotics (Greek 'xenos' = foreign) are compounds which are man-made and not produced by a biological procedure, and for which no equivalent exists in nature. They are subject to bioaccumulation, especially if fat soluble, as they get stored in the body fat of organisms, providing a route into the food chain. In gratuitous degradation, a xenobiotic resembles a natural compound so that it is recognised by the organism's enzymes and may be used as food. In cometabolism, a xenobiotic is degraded by the organism's enzymes but its catabolism does not provide energy, so it cannot be the sole carbon source.

subjective.question: How do endocrine disruptors such as oestrogens become reactivated in the environment?
subjective.answer: Natural oestrogens are deactivated in humans by glucuronidation, i.e. conjugation of the hormone with UDP-glucuronate, which makes the compound more polar and easily cleared from the blood by the kidneys. However, many bacteria have the enzyme β-glucuronidase, which removes this modification and thus reactivates the hormone. Raised levels of reactivated oestrogen in waterways lead to disturbances of the endocrine (hormonal) system in fauna, e.g. feminisation of male fish in many species including minnows, trout and flounders. Chemicals such as PAHs, DDT, alkyl phenols and some detergents may also mimic the activity of oestrogen.

subjective.question: Describe the degradation of polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) by Pseudomonas putida.
subjective.answer: Polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) are xenobiotics having a high level of halogenation, and they are substrates for very few pathways normally occurring in nature. A strain of Pseudomonas putida, isolated from waste water outflow from a refinery, is known to degrade PCBs. Two pathways are encoded by two separate operons: the tod pathway (employed in toluene degradation) and the cmt pathway (responsible for the catabolism of p-cumate). The mutation which allowed this strain to utilise the cmt pathway was found to be a single base change to the promoter-operator sequence.

subjective.topic: Mobility of DNA and Genetic Manipulation
subjective.question: Differentiate between conjugation, transduction and transformation.
subjective.answer: Conjugation is the genetic transfer through physical contact between bacteria. Transduction is the genetic transfer through bacteriophages (viruses that infect bacteria). Transformation is the taking up of foreign DNA by bacteria from their surroundings. Viruses and plasmids involved in such transfer are called extra-chromosomal elements.

subjective.topic: Mobility of DNA and Genetic Manipulation
subjective.question: What are transposons? What is their role in genome rearrangement?
subjective.answer: Transposons are pieces of DNA that stimulate the rearrangement of genomic material within an organism; they move from one point in the genome and reinsert into a second site, and the insertion may be into specific sites or random. Evolution occurs principally by insertions and deletions of genomes caused by such activities. Such activities can also rearrange existing structural genes into a different region of the genome, so that these genes operate under different parameters, affecting gene regulation.

subjective.topic: Mobility of DNA and Genetic Manipulation
subjective.question: How can bacteria be manipulated without genetic engineering to improve pollutant degradation?
subjective.answer: A sample of bacteria is taken from, at, or near the site of contamination, a pure culture is obtained in the laboratory and identified using standard microbiology techniques. The bacterium's tolerance to the pollutant may be increased by culturing it in growth medium containing increasing concentrations of the pollutant. In catabolic expansion, the microbe's ability to degrade a contaminant is improved by culturing the bacteria in a medium in which the contaminant is supplied as an essential part of the nutrition, so only bacteria that have undergone a mutation enabling them to utilise this food source survive. An increased rate of error (mutation) may be forced by including a mutagen in the growth medium. The 'trained' bacteria are then reintroduced to the polluted site, where they have an advantage over the indigenous bacteria.

subjective.topic: Mobility of DNA and Genetic Manipulation
subjective.question: What problems are associated with the use of genetically engineered microorganisms in the environment?
subjective.answer: Genetic manipulation by deliberate introduction of defined genes is powerful, but in practice very little environmental biotechnology relies directly on recombinants and transgenics, mainly because of cost. When a recombinant microbe is applied in bioaugmentation, it comes into competition with indigenous species which could outgrow it. The recombinant bacterium may also lose its new capability through the normal transfer of genes between bacteria. A highly controlled and contained environment such as a bioreactor may circumvent some of these objections. In reality, there is rarely any need to use recombinants or transgenics, as the required metabolic capability is mostly provided by indigenous organisms.

subjective.question: What are the fundamental requirements of all cloning procedures?
subjective.answer: The fundamental requirements of all cloning procedures are: (1) the enzymes, solutions and equipment necessary to perform the procedures; (2) the desired piece of DNA to be transferred; (3) a cloning vector; and (4) the recipient cell. It is also essential to have some means of determining whether or not the transfer has been successful, which is achieved by the use of marker genes.

subjective.question: Describe the role of restriction endonucleases and ligase in preparing recombinant DNA.
subjective.answer: Once DNA has been isolated and purified, it is cut for insertion into the vector by restriction digestion (or PCR). Restriction endonucleases recognise specific sequences within the DNA and cut at that site, producing either a flush/blunt end or a staggered ('sticky') end. Preparation of the vector is dictated by the type of end prepared for the insert DNA: if it is sticky, the appropriate sticky end must be prepared on the vector by a suitable restriction endonuclease. The prepared insert ('foreign' DNA) is then incubated with the prepared vector in an aqueous solution containing various salts and ligase enzyme, which sticks the pieces together to form the recombinant DNA molecule.

subjective.question: What is PCR and how does it work?
subjective.answer: The polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is a powerful technique which amplifies a piece of DNA of which only very few copies are available. The piece must be flanked by DNA of somewhat known sequence, so that short primer sequences can be synthesised to bind specifically to each end. The process works by constant cycling of: (1) denaturation of double stranded DNA at elevated temperature, approximately 95°C; (2) cooling to approximately 55-60°C to allow annealing of the primers; and (3) extension of the 3' end of the primer by DNA polymerase, usually at 72°C. PCR requires DNA polymerases able to withstand such treatment, e.g. Taq polymerase isolated from the thermophilic microorganism Thermus aquaticus.

subjective.question: Differentiate between genomic libraries and cDNA libraries.
subjective.answer: A genomic library is a collection of total genomic DNA from an organism: the genomic DNA is isolated, purified and cut into pieces of a size suitable for insertion into a cloning vector, followed by ligation and transformation into a host cell. If the genomic library is of eukaryotic origin, the genes will contain non-coding regions called introns (prokaryotes do not contain introns), which is a problem if the gene is to be expressed. This problem is avoided by using cDNA: cDNA is DNA artificially made using the mature mRNA as a template through the enzyme reverse transcriptase, so the synthetic DNA is simply a DNA version of the mRNA and contains no introns.

subjective.question: What is a cloning vector? Describe the role of selector marker genes and the multiple cloning site.
subjective.answer: A cloning vector is frequently a plasmid or a bacteriophage (bacterial virus). It must be fairly small and fully sequenced, and able to replicate itself when reintroduced into a host cell, thus producing large amounts of the recombinant DNA. It must also carry 'selector marker' genes, which are indicators of genomic integrity and activity. A common design carries two genes coding for antibiotic resistance; the 'foreign' gene is inserted within one of these genes so that it is no longer functional, making it possible to discriminate which bacteria carry recombinant DNA. Selector marker genes normally contain a multiple cloning site (MCS), a cluster of sites for restriction enzymes, which makes the manipulations easier.

subjective.question: What are expression vectors and reporter genes? Give examples of reporter genes.
subjective.answer: Expression vectors are similar to cloning vectors but additionally have the required regulatory regions located before and after the 'foreign' gene, which direct the host cell to translate the product of transcription into a protein. Reporter genes indicate whether or not the signals are 'switched on', allowing the 'foreign' DNA to be expressed. They usually code for a trait or an enzyme, e.g. an antibiotic resistance gene or β-galactosidase (used in Blue/White screening). Other reporter genes produce enzymes which cause the emission of light, such as the luciferase isolated from fireflies, or whose activity is easy and quick to assay, like the bacterial β-glucuronidase (GUS), which is probably the most frequently used reporter gene in transgenic plants.

subjective.question: Describe the steps involved in the analysis (screening) of recombinants.
subjective.answer: The design of the vector is such that the insertion of 'foreign' DNA allows for a colour test, or causes a change in antibiotic sensitivity; this constitutes the first step in screening. The second stage is usually to probe for the desired gene using molecules which will recognise it and to which some sort of tag is attached. The next stage is normally to analyze the DNA isolated from possible recombinants, firstly by checking the size of the molecule or pieces thereof, or by sequencing the DNA. If a large number of samples are to be analyzed, it is usually quicker and cheaper to scan them by Southern blotting, in which DNA fragments are resolved by electrophoresis on a gel, shifted to a membrane (nylon or nitrocellulose) and probed with a piece of DNA complementary to the sequence of interest; if a band shows up on autoradiography, the required sequences are present.

subjective.question: Differentiate between Southern, Northern and Western blotting.
subjective.answer: Southern blotting is used for the detection of specific DNA sequences: DNA fragments are resolved by electrophoresis on a gel, transferred to a nylon or nitrocellulose membrane and probed with complementary DNA. Northern blotting is the corresponding technique used for the detection of RNA. Western blotting is used for the detection of proteins, e.g. through antibody-antigen interaction.

subjective.question: Why has yeast become popular for cloning and expressing eukaryotic genes? How is DNA introduced into yeast cells?
subjective.answer: Yeast, being a unicellular eukaryote, has become popular for cloning and expressing eukaryotic genes; it is fairly simple to propagate, and some species are amenable to culture in much the same way as bacteria. Yeast cells are surrounded by a thick cell wall which must be removed to permit entry of DNA into the cell. Several types of plasmid vectors are available for genetic engineering of yeast, some constructed to allow replication in both bacteria and yeast; such vectors have a region which permits integration into the host yeast genome by recombination, in which two crossover events take place between homologous regions on the vector and the yeast genome.
